strengths: The paper presents a clean and well-motivated algebraic framework (Definitions 4.1-4.3) that unifies Laplace-like operators, diffusion operators, and smoothing operators under mass-weighted inner products, and convincingly shows that popular normalization schemes (row, symmetric, spectral) each violate some desired axiom.

The theoretical results are sound and well-executed: Theorem 4.1 (existence and uniqueness of the Sinkhorn scaling producing a diffusion operator) is proved rigorously via entropic optimal transport, and the damping property (spectrum in [0,1]) is established with an elegant sum-of-squares argument; Theorem 4.2 gives a fixed-kernel convergence guarantee for Gaussian/exponential kernels under weak convergence of discrete measures, complementing the sigma->0 manifold-learning literature.

The method is practical and scalable: the symmetric Sinkhorn loop is GPU-friendly, converges in 5-10 iterations, requires no factorizations, and admits an elegant attention-style implementation (Eq. 35-36) compatible with FlashAttention/xFormers, which is a genuinely useful engineering insight.

The paper is honestly scoped: the authors explicitly acknowledge that they do not prove convergence to a manifold Laplacian as sigma->0, that eigenvalue convergence is not established, and that experiments are preliminary. The supplementary material is thorough (full proofs, convergence curves, ablations on sigma, FEM reference details).

Broad applicability is demonstrated across data types (graphs, point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures) and tasks (spectral analysis, gradient flow preconditioning, LDDMM interpolation, point-cloud correspondence).
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental: symmetric Sinkhorn scaling is standard (Knight et al.), entropy-regularized OT normalization is standard (Feydy et al., Theorem 4.2 closely follows Theorem 1 of [34]), and bi-stochastic normalization of Laplacians/kernels is well studied ([58, 90, 23]). The main new ingredient is the mass-matrix/weighted-inner-product formulation, which is a relatively small delta over prior work.

Quantitative evaluation is thin. Most results (Figures 3-5, 7, 9-17) are qualitative visualizations. The single quantitative benchmark (Figure 6) shows Q-DiffNet is *worse* than mesh-based baselines on FAUST and SCAPE (2.1/2.4 vs 1.6/2.1) and only better on SHREC19 (3.5 vs 4.6), a modest and single-dataset gain that does not fully substantiate the 'broad applicability' claim.

There is no quantitative comparison against alternative point-cloud Laplacian constructions (e.g., point-cloud heat methods, [93], local kernel approximations) or against simple baselines such as iterated symmetric normalization; claims of superiority rest largely on visual inspection.

The spectral evidence shows divergence between volumetric and FEM eigenvalues around index 20, and eigenvalue estimation relies on heuristics (Eqs. 47-48) whose accuracy is not systematically quantified.

Reproducibility could be stronger: implementation details are provided, but no code release is explicitly promised, and several experimental choices (KDE for voxel masses, Q-DiffNet channel configuration) would be hard to reproduce exactly without code.

Some sections read more as a clarification/taxonomy of known normalizations than as a new method (the authors themselves describe the work as a 'clarification of the literature on graph Laplacians'), which limits the significance of the theoretical contribution relative to ICML's bar.

strengths: Well-written and pedagogically clear: the warm-up on graphs (Section 3) and the axiomatic definitions of Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators (Section 4) effectively clarify how row, symmetric, spectral, and bi-stochastic normalizations trade off symmetry, mass conservation, and positivity.

The theory is technically correct. Theorem 4.1 (existence/uniqueness of the diagonal scaling) and Theorem 4.2 (convergence of discrete operators to a continuous diffusion operator under a fixed kernel scale) are sound, with proofs in the appendix that are largely faithful adaptations of known entropic-OT results (Feydy et al. [34], Knight & Ruiz [50]).

The authors are unusually honest about scope: they explicitly state they do not prove convergence to a manifold Laplacian as sigma -> 0, nor convergence of eigenvalues, and they acknowledge the experiments 'remain preliminary'.

The algorithm is simple, GPU-friendly (matrix-vector products only, compatible with KeOps/FlashAttention via a softmax reformulation), and the appended convergence curves (Figure 7) show Sinkhorn iterations converge in ~5-10 steps.

Broad set of application sketches (spectral analysis across point clouds/voxels/Gaussian mixtures, gradient-flow preconditioning, LDDMM shape interpolation, and a DiffusionNet-style shape matching network) that together demonstrate the operator is genuinely plug-and-play across representations.
weaknesses: Limited theoretical novelty. Theorem 4.1 is essentially the classical symmetric Sinkhorn scaling of Knight & Ruiz [50] (the paper itself says Algorithm 1 is 'directly equivalent to Eq. (25) in [34]') combined with a short spectral argument. Theorem 4.2 is a direct application of Theorem 1 in Feydy et al. [34], with the proof remarking that 'the hypotheses fit perfectly'. The genuinely new ingredient — inserting a mass matrix M into the inner product — is a modest delta over bi-stochastic normalization already studied for manifold learning [58, 90, 23].

The key empirical question — does exact mass preservation materially improve results over one iteration of symmetric normalization, which the authors themselves note already achieves 1-5% constant-preservation error — is never answered with a controlled ablation. Downstream baselines only compare against unnormalized kernels, not against row- or symmetric-normalized alternatives.

The headline deep learning result is mixed: Q-DiffNet (2.1/2.4 mean geodesic error on FAUST/SCAPE) is worse than the mesh-based DiffNet (1.6/2.2) and ULRSSM (1.6/2.1) baselines, and roughly ties the point-cloud ULRSSM retraining (2.3/2.4), with a gain only on SHREC19 (3.5 vs 5.1). This supports 'usable on point clouds' more than 'better', and the advantage is confined to one of three test sets.

The gradient-flow (Figure 4) and LDDMM (Figure 5) experiments are qualitative demonstrations on single examples without quantitative metrics, multiple seeds, or comparisons to established alternatives — insufficient evidence for claims such as 'provides an elegant solution' to contraction-expansion dynamics of kernel metrics.
Claims of scalability ('scaled to millions of points') are asserted but never demonstrated: no runtimes, no memory measurements, no large-scale experiment anywhere in the paper or appendix.

Sensitivity to nonuniform sampling density is not analyzed. Prior work on bi-stochastic normalization [90, 23] shows robustness properties in the sigma -> 0 regime precisely because this matters; in the fixed-kernel regime adopted here, the behavior of Q under clustered or nonuniform masses is left unexamined.
The eigenvalue estimation heuristics (Eqs. 47-48) are ad hoc, calibrated to isotropic/surface-covariance assumptions, and their accuracy is not validated against ground truth.
No explicit code-release statement, which, combined with preliminary experiments, limits reproducibility of the empirical claims.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and pedagogically structured; the warm-up on graphs (Section 3) and Figure 2 make the trade-offs between row, symmetric, spectral, and Sinkhorn normalizations very easy to grasp.

The core construction is elegant: using a domain-specific mass matrix M so that symmetric Sinkhorn scaling yields an operator Q = ΛSΛ that is simultaneously mass-preserving, symmetric under the M-weighted inner product, entrywise positive, and spectrally damped (eigenvalues in [0,1]). The proof of the spectral bound (Eq. 19–22, supplementary) is elementary and self-contained.

The framing as an axiomatic framework (Definitions 4.1–4.3) cleanly unifies Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators and situates classical normalizations as special cases, which is useful conceptual clarification.

Theory is honest about scope: Theorem 4.2 gives a fixed-σ convergence guarantee (complementary to the σ→0 manifold-learning results of Wormell & Reich and Cheng & Landa), and the paper explicitly states what is NOT proven (convergence to a true manifold Laplacian, eigenvalue convergence).

Implementation is practical and scalable: matrix-vector-product formulation, log-domain stability via KeOps, attention-layer compatibility (Eq. 35–36), sparse volumes via Taichi; Sinkhorn converges in 5–10 iterations across settings (Figure 7).

The paper covers diverse data modalities (graphs, point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures) within one framework, including a nontrivial extension of the kernel to full covariance matrices (Eq. 6).

Reproducibility is well supported: extensive supplementary details on all experiments, datasets, training setups, and library dependencies; limitations (preliminary experiments, scalability) are candidly acknowledged in the conclusion.
weaknesses: Theoretical novelty is incremental. The main tools — symmetric Sinkhorn scaling (Knight–Ruiz), the entropic OT formulation, and the convergence argument — are directly imported from Feydy et al. [34] and [50]. The genuinely new element is the M-weighted variant and its geometric interpretation; Theorem 4.2 is essentially an instantiation of Theorem 1 in [34]. Reviewers may judge the contribution as more of a careful adaptation than a new technique.

The damping property for the continuous limit operator Q in Theorem 4.2 is asserted 'from the fact that we can write Q as the limit of discrete diffusion operators with eigenvalues in [0,1]', but eigenvalue/spectrum convergence is explicitly not proven. The argument needs an operator-norm continuity statement for M-self-adjoint operators to be rigorous.

Experimental evidence is thin and mostly qualitative. The spectral analysis (Figure 3, 8–14) shows agreement only for low modes, with divergence around index 20 and 'simple heuristics' for eigenvalue estimation (Eq. 47–48) that are ad hoc. The gradient-flow and LDDMM experiments are single visual examples without quantitative metrics, baselines, or sensitivity analyses.

The deep learning results are mixed: Q-DiffNet does not consistently outperform point-cloud baselines on FAUST and SCAPE (e.g., 2.1/2.4 vs 2.3/2.4 for ULRSSM-PC, and worse than DiffNet-PC on FAUST), and only clearly wins on SHREC19. No error bars, multiple seeds, or statistical significance are reported; the advantage could be within run-to-run variance.

Missing ablations: no study of sensitivity to the kernel scale σ (the key hyperparameter), robustness to noise/outliers/sampling density, or runtime comparison against the spectral and implicit-Euler baselines that the paper criticizes. The claim that the method scales 'to millions of points' is asserted but never demonstrated experimentally.

Positioning relative to closest related work could be sharper: bi-stochastically normalized graph Laplacians ([58, 90, 23]) already use the same scaling machinery, and the paper's distinct contribution (mass-weighted vs doubly stochastic) deserves a more direct empirical comparison to those baselines, rather than only row/symmetric/spectral normalizations.

Some of the claimed motivation (e.g., applications to Gaussian splats, medical imaging) is aspirational; the experiments are on standard well-studied shapes (Armadillo, sphere, cube, FAUST/SCAPE/SHREC), so the strongest claimed use cases for unstructured data are not actually evaluated.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: bringing heat-diffusion-like smoothing to unstructured geometric data (point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids) where Laplacians are unavailable or unreliable, and diagnosing precisely why raw kernels, row/symmetric normalizations, and spectral truncation each fail (Figure 2).

Sound theoretical framework: the axiomatic definitions of Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators are clean, and Theorem 4.4 (existence/uniqueness of the symmetric Sinkhorn scaling yielding a valid diffusion operator), Theorem 4.5 (stability at fixed kernel scale under sampling refinement), and Proposition 4.6 (error damping by factor ≥ 2 in scaling factors under mass perturbation) are correct and relevant. The proofs in Sections B–D are carefully written, and the authors are transparent that the machinery builds on Feydy et al. (2019) and Knight et al. (2014).

Distinct positioning from the manifold-learning literature (Marshall & Coifman, Wormell & Reich, Cheng & Landa): the focus is on the bounded diffusion operator Q itself at a fixed practical scale rather than the asymptotic differential operator, which is the right target for geometry-processing applications.

Broad and convincing empirical validation: spectral consistency across modalities (Figures 3, 8, 11–14), stability under severe non-uniform downsampling (Figure 9), gradient-flow improvement (Figures 4, 15–18), LDDMM pose interpolation with quantitative area-distortion analysis (Figures 5, 19, 20), runtime benchmarks on up to 1M points (Tables 1, 3), and a shape-correspondence experiment where Q-DiffNet outperforms point-cloud baselines and matches/beats mesh upper bounds on SHREC19 (Table 2), with an honest XYZ-input ablation (Table 4) showing feature-engineering effects.

Thoughtful practical details: equivalence to symmetric Sinkhorn on MKM, attention/FlashAttention-compatible formulation (Eq. 37–39), generalized eigenproblem reformulation for M-symmetric operators, KeOps/attention scalability, and convergence-rate analysis (Figure 7). Code is promised, and implementation details are thorough enough to support reproducibility.
Honest limitations section discussing dependence on mass-matrix quality, strictness of mass preservation, and weaker theoretical guarantees on unstructured data.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty in the technical core: the symmetric Sinkhorn algorithm is Knight et al. (2014), and the existence/uniqueness and convergence arguments in Theorems 4.4 and 4.5 are largely direct reformulations of entropic OT results in Feydy et al. (2019) (Section C states the hypotheses 'fit perfectly' with prior work). The genuinely new theoretical content reduces mainly to the fixed-scale framing, the positivity/axiom checking, and the stability bound of Proposition 4.6 — modest for a main-track paper, though the integration into geometry processing is a real contribution.

The assumption of strictly positive entries in S (Theorem 4.4) is restrictive for the application domain: sparse graphs and k-NN kernels (used in the runtime benchmarks, Table 3) require the ε = 1·1^T regularization trick, which changes the operator, and the paper only points to Knight et al. (2014) for the zero-entry case rather than analyzing it.

The claim that Q's spectrum 'approximates the exponential of a Laplacian' is supported empirically (Figure 3) via heuristic eigenvalue recovery formulas (Eqs. 50–51) rather than proven; deviations are visible in all spectral plots, and the appendix acknowledges only a 'weak' link to a continuous Laplace–Beltrami operator on unstructured data.

Some experiments are qualitative or limited in scale: gradient-flow and LDDMM results involve single shape pairs, and the correspondence benchmark gains on FAUST/SCAPE are marginal (2.1 vs 2.3), with the strongest gain (SHREC19) partly attributable to missing-data robustness rather than the operator itself.

Minor presentation issues: several typos ('if preserved' in the abstract, 'variant exits', 'botter'), an empty code URL placeholder, and Figures 13/14 have duplicated captions with inconsistent content ('cube with edge length 1' for both, one apparently depicting a sphere), suggesting insufficient proofreading of the supplementary material.

strengths: Technically solid core contribution: the axiomatic framework (Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators, Definitions 4.1-4.3) is clean, and Theorem 4.4 (existence/uniqueness of the symmetric Sinkhorn scaling producing a valid diffusion operator) plus the spectral bound proof in Section B are correct and self-contained.

Theorem 4.5 (fixed-bandwidth convergence under refinement) addresses a practically relevant regime that is distinct from the N→∞, σ→0 asymptotics of the manifold-learning literature (Wormell & Reich 2021; Cheng & Landa 2024), and the positioning against that literature is explicit and fair.

Broad empirical validation across modalities (meshes, point clouds, Gaussian mixtures, voxel grids, graphs), with quantitative evidence: eigenvalue/eigenvector consistency (Figures 3, 8, 11-14), stability to sampling density (Figure 9), runtime benchmarks on GPU and CPU (Tables 1, 3), and an empirical confirmation of the perturbation bound in Proposition 4.6 (Figure 6).

The Q-DiffNet experiments are thoughtfully designed to isolate the operator contribution (all methods receive identical mesh-derived WKS descriptors), and Q-DiffNet beats the point-cloud baselines on FAUST/SCAPE and outperforms even mesh-based upper bounds on SHREC19 (Table 2); the XYZ-only ablation (Table 4) is an honest additional control.

Honest and substantive limitations section covering dependence on the mass matrix, the possible suboptimality of strict mass preservation, and the weaker theoretical link to a 'true' Laplacian on unstructured data.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: symmetric Sinkhorn normalization and its convergence theory are well established (Knight et al. 2014; Feydy et al. 2019, whose proofs the paper directly reuses for Theorems 4.4-4.5; Marshall & Coifman 2019; Wormell & Reich 2021; Cheng & Landa 2024). The contribution is largely a re-framing (fixed-scale, axiomatic, geometry-processing-oriented) and an engineering effort rather than new mathematical substance.

The central downstream experiments are not fully unstructured: the correspondence pipeline still relies on mesh-derived WKS descriptors and, for the main Q-DiffNet variant, mesh Laplacian eigenvectors in the functional-map losses (Appendix J), so the claim of 'Laplacian-like smoothing on unstructured data' is only partially realized in the strongest results.

Some evidence is qualitative where quantitative comparisons would be expected: the gradient-flow and LDDMM improvements (Figures 4-5) rest on a single Chamfer-distance curve and area-distortion plots with limited baselines and no statistical rigor; the authors themselves note they had to hand-rescale the unnormalized baseline's learning rate, weakening the comparison.

Presentation defects: Figures 13 and 14 have identical captions for what appear to be different shapes; several typos ('botter', 'if preserved', 'use use', 'variant exits'); code links are left blank in the manuscript, undermining reproducibility claims at review time.

Comparison to the closest baselines is incomplete: normalized graph attention or bi-stochastic-kernel methods (Marshall & Coifman 2019) are discussed but not empirically compared on the correspondence or flow tasks; only DiffusionNet/ULRSSM retrainings serve as competitors.

The stability analysis (Proposition 4.6) is first-order only; its practical relevance given badly misestimated masses, acknowledged as a limitation, is not stress-tested beyond log-normal noise on a single shape.

strengths: Well-motivated problem: transferring heat-diffusion-like smoothing to unstructured geometric data (point clouds, voxel grids, Gaussian mixtures) that lack a Laplacian, addressing a genuine gap between differential-geometry tools and practical irregular data.

Coherent axiomatic framework: the paper cleanly defines Laplace-like, diffusion, and smoothing operators (Defs. 4.1-4.3) and shows how row/symmetric/spectral normalizations each fail a subset of desirable axioms, motivating Sinkhorn normalization as the unique fix.

Solid and mostly self-contained theory: Theorem 4.4 (existence and uniqueness of a symmetric, mass-preserving rescaling) is proved rigorously via entropy-regularized OT duality; Theorem 4.5 (convergence under sampling refinement at fixed bandwidth) and Proposition 4.6 (stability of scaling factors to mass perturbations, with the elegant 1/2 damping factor) are meaningful additions beyond the asymptotic manifold-learning literature, and the proofs in the appendix are careful and credible.

Breadth of empirical validation: spectral consistency across modalities against FEM/cotan references (Figs. 3, 8, 11-14), stability to non-uniform sampling (Fig. 9), gradient-flow stabilization (Figs. 4, 15-18), LDDMM interpolation improvements with quantitative area-distortion analysis (Fig. 19), and integration into DiffusionNet/ULRSSM for shape correspondence, where Q-DiffNet beats point-cloud baselines and even mesh upper bounds on SHREC19 (Table 2).

Practical, GPU-friendly implementation: black-box matvec formulation compatible with KeOps/FlashAttention, extensive runtime benchmarks (Tables 1 and 3), honest treatment of complexity of competing Laplacian-based baselines (Sec. F).

Honest and thoughtful limitations section (dependence on mass matrix quality, strict mass preservation not always optimal, weaker continuous-Laplacian guarantees on unstructured data), plus a relevant ablation (XYZ inputs) that guards against overclaiming.
Good reproducibility: code is stated to be released, hyperparameters and training setups are specified in detail (Sec. J), and datasets/protocols follow standard splits.
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: the central mechanism (symmetric Sinkhorn/bi-stochastic normalization of kernel matrices) is well established (Knight et al., 2014; Marshall & Coifman, 2019; Wormell & Reich, 2021; Cheng & Landa, 2024), and the paper's fixed-scale focus, while a genuine repositioning, means the main theorems largely repackage known OT results. The contribution is more a careful synthesis plus applications than a fundamentally new technique.

Theorem 4.5 requires strictly positive kernel entries; for sparse structures (e.g., graphs, k-NN kernels) the construction needs the regularization A + eps*11^T, which is a somewhat ad hoc patch, and behavior with zero entries is delegated to prior work rather than analyzed here.

The axiomatic framework is convincing but partially arbitrary: the choice of exactly these four axioms, and the claim that Sinkhorn normalization is the principled answer, is argued informally rather than derived from a uniqueness or optimality characterization (beyond existence/uniqueness of the scaling).

Several application results are qualitative or modest: the shape correspondence gains on FAUST/SCAPE are on par with baselines (2.1 vs 2.3), and gradient-flow/LDDMM experiments are on small synthetic or few-shape examples without broader benchmarking.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('if preserved', 'botter', 'exits'), a broken/missing code URL in the abstract, and some notation-heavy passages (Sec. 4) that could slow readers outside the geometry processing community.
The link between estimated Laplacian eigenvalues from Q and true Laplacian spectra relies on heuristics (Eqs. 50-51) whose accuracy conditions are not fully characterized.
